concepts.hook: A nanny goat who finds the first safe ledge when the snow leaves the cliffs, and the herders follow her line up into spring.
At midsummer shearing the sky-ewe lies with her fleece pulled off and the wool hung along the Lamp Road to dry, so the summer sky smells of lanolin.
A stoat that turns white at the first frost and runs the Lamp Road all winter, visible only by the black tip of its tail, so children are told to keep quiet when they see it.
Lemmings that march off the cliff-edge in a bad year, and Kael's net is said to be strung beneath them, though it has never once held anything.
Puffins return to their burrows each spring, and the children count them with pebbles, and each year Hesk is asked which of them did not come back.
A man hangs over the sea-cliff on a rope in early summer, cutting eggs from the guillemot ledges, and the knot he ties is one no one has ever cut.
An eider hen plucks the down from her own breast to line the nest, and the sky shows her bare and patient, which the old women say is how a mother should wait.
Geese that leave in a wedge each autumn for the warm water past the Leeward Reach, and the wedge is said to point the way a drowned boat should have come home.
The first small bird back from the south in late winter, and whoever sees it first is owed a meal by the household.
A broody hen who sits on the lightning eggs, and when she shifts her weight the spring storms come round the islands.
Herring come in autumn in a shoal so thick the boats are said to sail on it, and the nets are hung under the Lamp Road to remember the catch.
A deep-water squid that carries its own light and blinks it at passing boats, which is why the fishermen say the Lamp Road is a shoal that remembers how to shine.
Children count the limpets on the rocks at the spring low tide, and Hesk is said to keep the same tally in the sky, where the number never changes.
Long brown kelp that stands up in the cold current with its hair loose, and the fisher women tie their lines to her before a storm.
A pink flower that grows in a crack of the cliff in early summer, the first colour the islands see after the grey.
Sorrel leaves picked in spring and eaten against the gum-rot of the long winter, the plant that brings the blood back.
Men cut heather in late summer for thatch and bedding, and the sky shows the curved shape of the sickle where the cut was made.
A pale trunk of a tree no one on the islands grows, washed up from the far south, and it is said to have come from the Unflown.
A figure with a seed-basket who scatters hail across the spring fields, and the houses bring their sacks in when they see her arm go up.
A bank of sea-fog that comes off the water and grazes slowly along the Lamp Road, and the goats must be brought in when she bleats.
A sea eel with a mouth like a torn net that takes hooks and lines whole, leaving the boats with nothing but frayed rope.
A thin grey climber that goes up the sea-cliffs in the dark months and taps at the shutters, and families leave a bowl of goat's milk on the step.
A tall figure with driftwood stilts that walks the mud at the lowest ebb, counting who is out past the rocks.
A grey seal who lifts her head at every burial on the shore and sings one low note that makes the mourners stop talking.
A cuckoo that lays her egg in another bird's nest, and the sky shows the foster bird feeding a chick that is not its own.
A grey heron standing still as a mooring post through the whole of the ebb, and whoever stands that long at a kelp pool is said to get the best fish.
White seed-heads of bog cotton picked in winter to stuff pillows, the soft thing the poor sleep on.
Cod split and hung on racks in the frost, a row of stiff fish turning slowly as the wind works the salt into them.
A slender birch the islanders plant for a newborn, which grows as the child grows, and its pale trunk rises beside the Lamp Road each spring.
A tern that rides the gale farther than any other bird, and Tavo is said to laugh when it is caught and carried off the road.
